## Overview

The Potiguara, also called Potyguara or Pitiguara, are an Indigenous people of Brazil. They live in Paraíba, in the municipalities of Marcação, Baía da Traição and Rio Tinto. Their population numbers sixteen thousand individuals, who occupy 26 villages in 3 Indigenous reservations: Potiguara, Jacaré de São Domingos and Potiguara de Monte-Mor. According to José de Alencar, their name means “shrimp-eaters,” from *poty*, “shrimp,” and *uara*, “eater.” The sources connect Potiguara history with Brazil’s colonial period, the Portuguese, the Dutch invasions and the military service of António Filipe Camarão. Their linguistic context is associated with Old Tupi, a classical Tupian language belonging to the Tupi–Guarani language family.

## Foodways

The sources state that the name Potiguara means “shrimp-eaters,” according to José de Alencar, deriving it from *poty*, “shrimp,” and *uara*, “eater.”

## Oral tradition & literature

The Old Tupi material states that the language has a rich literature including catechisms, poems and plays, and that José de Anchieta reportedly wrote more than 4,000 lines of poetry in tupinambá.

## Language & religion

The source titled “Potiguara language” describes Old Tupi, also called Ancient Tupi or Classical Tupi, as a classical Tupian language belonging to the Tupi–Guarani language family. It says that Old Tupi was spoken by Indigenous Tupi people of Brazil, had a written history spanning the 16th, 17th and early 18th centuries, and was used as a lingua franca in the early colonial period before later being suppressed almost to extinction. The source discusses Tupi phonology, grammar, literature and historical documentation, including works associated with André Thévet, José de Anchieta, Jean de Lery and Luís Figueira.
